title: Area, Perimeter and Volume
bigQuestion: How can counting squares and cubes tell us how much space a shape takes up?

story.title: The Garden That Needed a Fence
story.kicker: A class wants to plant a garden, but first they must answer two very different questions about the same rectangle.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz's fourth graders won a small grant to build a garden behind their school on the South Side of Chicago. The custodian marked out a rectangle on the grass with string. It was 8 feet long and 5 feet wide. Everyone cheered. Then Ms. Ortiz asked two questions. How much fence do we need? How many seed packets do we need?

Jamal thought the two questions had the same answer. The garden is one rectangle, so one number should describe it. But when the class walked the string, they counted 8 steps, then 5, then 8, then 5. That was 26 feet of edge. The fence needed to go all the way around, so the fence question was about the *distance around*.

The seed question was different. Each seed packet covers one square foot of dirt. Priya drew the garden on grid paper, one square for each square foot. She counted 5 rows with 8 squares in each row. That made 40 squares. The garden needed 40 packets, not 26. The seed question was about the space inside, not the edge.

Later the class found that a 10 by 4 garden also uses 40 packets but needs 28 feet of fence. A 20 by 2 garden uses 40 packets and needs 44 feet of fence. Same inside, different edge. When the raised beds arrived and needed soil, a third question appeared: how many cubic feet of dirt fill a box? That is the question this chapter ends on.
story.think: Why did the fence question and the seed question have different answers when they were about the same garden?

lessons.title: Area Is Counting Squares
lessons.mainIdea: Area is the number of unit squares that cover a flat shape with no gaps and no overlaps.
reading: Imagine a kitchen floor covered with square tiles, each tile 1 foot on a side. If you count the tiles, you know how much floor there is. Mathematicians call that count the *area*. A *unit square* is a square with sides of 1 unit. Area tells how many unit squares fit inside a shape.

Try a rectangle drawn on grid paper. It is 4 squares tall and 6 squares wide. Count row by row: 6, 12, 18, 24. The rectangle covers 24 unit squares. We write the area as 24 *square units*. If each square is 1 centimeter wide, the area is 24 square centimeters.

Two rules matter. The squares must cover the whole shape with no gaps. The squares must not overlap. A common mistake is counting only the squares along the edge. Those squares are the border, not the inside. Count every square that fits inside, including the ones in the middle.

words.d: the number of unit squares that cover a flat shape
a square with sides that are each 1 unit long, like 1 inch or 1 foot
the label for area; 24 square units means 24 unit squares fit inside

look.title: Count the Tiles
look.text: Picture a rectangle on grid paper. It has 3 rows. Each row holds 7 squares. Count the first row: 7. Add the second row: 14. Add the third row: 21. The rectangle has an area of 21 square units. Now picture a different rectangle with 5 rows of 4 squares.
look.prompt: What is the area of the 5-row rectangle? Count the rows out loud, adding 4 each time.

check.q: A rectangle on grid paper has 3 rows of 5 unit squares. What is its area?
check.why: Count 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 unit squares. Adding 3 + 5 gives 8, which is not area.

check.q: Which label belongs on an area?
check.why: Area counts unit squares, so it is labeled in square units like square inches.

check.q: One shape covers 12 unit squares. Another covers 9. How many more squares does the first cover?
check.why: Subtract: 12 − 9 = 3. Adding gives 21, which answers a different question.

lessons.title: Multiply Rows and Columns
lessons.mainIdea: The area of a rectangle equals its length times its width, because the rows repeat the same count.
reading: Counting squares one at a time is slow for a big garden. Look at the rows instead. A garden bed that is 7 feet wide and 8 feet long has 7 rows of squares. Each row has 8 squares. That is 7 groups of 8, which is a multiplication problem: 7 × 8 = 56. The area is 56 square feet.

This works for every rectangle. Call one side the *length* and the other the *width*. The area is length × width. The rule is a *formula*: a short sentence in symbols that always works. Area = length × width. For a rectangle 9 cm by 6 cm, the area is 9 × 6 = 54 square centimeters.

Check the formula by counting. A 3 by 4 rectangle has rows of 4, 4, 4. Adding gives 12. Multiplying 3 × 4 also gives 12. Multiplication is just fast adding of equal rows. One common mistake is to add the sides instead: 3 + 4 = 7. Adding gives you part of the border, not the area.

words.d: the longer side of a rectangle, or the side you choose to measure first
the side of a rectangle that meets the length at a corner
a rule written in symbols that always works, like Area = length × width

look.title: Rows in a Garden
look.text: A garden bed is 6 feet by 9 feet. Draw it as 6 rows of 9 squares. You could add 9 six times: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54. Or you could multiply: 6 × 9 = 54. Both give 54 square feet. Now try a bed that is 4 feet by 12 feet.
look.prompt: Find the area of the 4 by 12 bed both ways. Which way was faster, and why?

check.q: A rectangle is 9 units long and 6 units wide. What is its area?
check.why: Multiply 9 × 6 = 54. Adding 9 + 6 = 15 is the mistake of adding instead of multiplying.

check.q: A square has sides of 7 inches. What is its area?
check.why: A square has equal sides, so 7 × 7 = 49 square inches. 28 is the perimeter.

check.q: A poster is 8 cm by 12 cm. Which sentence is true?
check.why: 8 × 12 = 96. Adding 8 + 12 gives 20, and 84 or 108 come from multiplication slips.

lessons.title: Choosing a Square Unit
lessons.mainIdea: Pick a square unit that fits the size of the thing: small squares for small things, big squares for big spaces.
reading: A postage stamp and a soccer field both have area, but you would not measure them the same way. Measure small things in *square centimeters* or square inches. Measure rooms in square feet or *square meters*. Measure whole cities in *square miles*. The unit matches the size of the thing.

Bigger units hold many smaller ones. A square foot is 12 inches by 12 inches. So it holds 12 × 12 = 144 square inches. A square yard is 3 feet by 3 feet, so it holds 3 × 3 = 9 square feet. Notice that the numbers get squared, not just multiplied by 12 or 3. That surprises many students.

Try a classroom rug that is 6 feet by 9 feet. Its area is 54 square feet. In square inches, the rug is 72 inches by 108 inches, which is 7,776 square inches. Both numbers describe the same rug. The square foot answer is easier to picture, so it is the better choice here.

words.d: the area of a square that is 1 centimeter on each side, good for small objects
the area of a square that is 1 meter on each side, good for rooms and yards
the area of a square that is 1 mile on each side, used for cities and states

look.title: How Many Small Squares Fit
look.cite: Standard U.S. customary and metric unit relationships
look.prompt: Why does 1 square foot hold 144 square inches and not 12? Draw a 12 by 12 grid to explain.

check.q: Which unit fits best for the area of a sticker?
check.why: A sticker is tiny, so a tiny unit like the square centimeter matches it.

check.q: How many square inches are in 1 square foot?
check.why: A square foot is 12 inches by 12 inches, so 12 × 12 = 144 square inches.

check.q: A rug is 2 yards by 3 yards. What is its area in square feet?
check.why: 2 yards is 6 feet and 3 yards is 9 feet, so 6 × 9 = 54. Multiplying 2 × 3 = 6 gives square yards, not square feet.

lessons.title: Perimeter Is Adding Sides
lessons.mainIdea: Perimeter is the total distance around a shape, found by adding the lengths of all its sides.
reading: Walk the string around the class garden. It is 8 feet, then 5 feet, then 8 feet, then 5 feet. The whole walk is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 feet. That distance around is the *perimeter*. A fence, a picture frame or a ribbon around a box all follow the perimeter.

Perimeter works for any shape with straight sides. A triangle with sides 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm has a perimeter of 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 cm. A five-sided park with sides 30, 40, 20, 40 and 30 meters has a perimeter of 160 meters. Add every side, and do not skip any.

Perimeter is measured in plain units like feet or centimeters, not square units. That is because it is a length, a line you could walk. A common mistake is to add only the two sides you can see labeled. In a rectangle, the unlabeled sides match the labeled ones. A 6 by 4 rectangle has sides 6, 4, 6 and 4.

words.d: the distance all the way around the outside of a shape
one straight edge of a shape; a triangle has 3 sides and a rectangle has 4

look.title: Walk the Edge
look.text: A playground is shaped like a rectangle, 20 meters by 12 meters. Picture walking the edge. You walk 20 meters, turn, walk 12, turn, walk 20, turn, walk 12. The total walk is 20 + 12 + 20 + 12 = 64 meters. Now picture a triangle-shaped flower bed with sides 3 m, 4 m and 5 m.
look.prompt: What is the perimeter of the triangle bed? How many sides did you add?

check.q: A rectangle is 8 feet by 3 feet. What is its perimeter?
check.why: Add all four sides: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22. Adding only 8 + 3 = 11 misses two sides.

check.q: A triangle has sides of 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. What is its perimeter?
check.why: 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm. Multiplying 6 × 8 = 48 is an area-style mistake.

check.q: A square has sides of 9 inches. What is its perimeter?
check.why: Four equal sides: 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 36 inches. 81 is the area, 9 × 9.

lessons.title: A Shortcut for Rectangles
lessons.mainIdea: For a rectangle, add length and width, then double: perimeter = 2 × (length + width).
reading: A rectangle has two lengths and two widths. So instead of adding four numbers, add length and width once, then *double* it. For a 12 by 5 rectangle, 12 + 5 = 17, and 17 doubled is 34. The perimeter is 34 units. Check the long way: 12 + 5 + 12 + 5 = 34. Same answer.

Written as a formula: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). The parentheses mean add first, then multiply. If you multiply first, 2 × 12 + 5 = 29, which is wrong. Another correct way is 2 × length + 2 × width, which is 24 + 10 = 34.

The shortcut helps with costs. The class garden is 10 feet by 7 feet. Fence costs $3 per foot. First find the perimeter: 10 + 7 = 17, doubled is 34 feet. Then find the cost: 34 × $3 = $102. A student who used the area, 70 square feet, would buy far too much fence.

words.d: to multiply by 2, or add a number to itself
the curved marks ( ) that show which part of a problem to do first

look.title: Fence for the Bed
look.text: A raised bed is 15 feet by 4 feet. Add the length and width: 15 + 4 = 19. Double it: 2 × 19 = 38 feet of edge. Fence boards cost $2 per foot, so the fence costs 38 × $2 = $76. Now imagine the bed is made longer, to 15 feet by 6 feet.
look.prompt: What is the new perimeter, and how much does the fence cost now? How much extra is that?

check.q: Which expression gives the perimeter of a 15 by 4 rectangle?
check.why: Add the length and width, then double: 2 × (15 + 4) = 2 × 19 = 38.

check.q: A garden is 10 feet by 7 feet. Fence costs $3 per foot. What does the fence cost?
check.why: Perimeter is 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 feet. Then 34 × $3 = $102. $70 is the area, not the fence.

check.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 26 units and a width of 5 units. What is its length?
check.why: Half of 26 is 13, which is length + width. Then 13 − 5 = 8.

lessons.title: Same Area, Different Fence
lessons.mainIdea: Two rectangles can have the same area but different perimeters, so you must find each one separately.
reading: Suppose the class has exactly 12 seed packets, one per square foot. Many rectangles have an area of 12 square feet. A 1 by 12 bed does. So does a 2 by 6 bed and a 3 by 4 bed. Each uses all 12 packets. But how much fence does each need?

Find each perimeter. The 1 by 12 bed: 2 × (1 + 12) = 26 feet. The 2 by 6 bed: 2 × (2 + 6) = 16 feet. The 3 by 4 bed: 2 × (3 + 4) = 14 feet. Same area, three different perimeters. The long skinny bed needs almost twice the fence of the nearly square bed.

The rule goes the other way, too. Two rectangles with the same perimeter can have different areas. A 1 by 7 rectangle and a 4 by 4 square both have a perimeter of 16. Their areas are 7 and 16. Shapes closest to a *square* give the most area for the least fence. That is why so many gardens and rooms are almost square.

words.d: a rectangle whose four sides are all the same length
to look at two things and tell how they are alike and how they differ

look.title: Beds With 24 Square Feet
look.cite: Perimeters computed from 2 × (length + width) for each bed of area 24 square feet
look.prompt: Every bed in the table has the same area. Which needs the least fence, and what do you notice about its shape?

check.q: Which rectangle with an area of 16 square units has the smallest perimeter?
choices: They all have the same perimeter.
check.why: Perimeters are 34, 20 and 16. The 4 by 4 square needs the least edge.

check.q: Which pair of rectangles has the same area?
check.why: 3 × 8 = 24 and 4 × 6 = 24. The other pairs give 10 and 12, 25 and 24, 10 and 12.

check.q: Two rectangles both have a perimeter of 16. One is 1 by 7 and one is 4 by 4. Which is true?
check.why: Areas are 1 × 7 = 7 and 4 × 4 = 16. Same perimeter, different areas.

lessons.title: Split It Into Rectangles
lessons.mainIdea: To find the area of an L-shape or T-shape, cut it into rectangles, find each area, and add.
reading: Not every garden is a rectangle. The class wants an L-shaped bed that wraps around a corner. There is no single formula for an L. But an L is just two rectangles stuck together. Cut it into pieces you know, find each area, and add them. This is called finding the area of a *composite* shape.

Picture an L made of a 10 by 4 rectangle with a 6 by 3 rectangle attached below its left end. The first piece has area 10 × 4 = 40. The second piece has area 6 × 3 = 18. Add them: 40 + 18 = 58 square feet. The line where you cut does not change the total area.

Sometimes it is easier to subtract. A 6 by 6 square with a 2 by 3 notch cut from one corner has area 36 − 6 = 30. Either way, the key idea is *decompose*: break the hard shape into easy pieces. A common mistake is counting the shared edge twice or forgetting one piece. Label each piece before you add.

words.d: a shape made by putting two or more simple shapes together
to break a shape or number into smaller parts that are easier to work with

look.title: The Corner Bed
look.text: An L-shaped bed has a top piece that is 5 feet by 3 feet. A second piece, 2 feet by 4 feet, hangs down from the right end. Find each area: 5 × 3 = 15 and 2 × 4 = 8. Add: 15 + 8 = 23 square feet. Now picture a T-shape: a 9 by 2 bar across the top and a 3 by 5 stem below it.
look.prompt: What is the area of the T-shaped bed? Which two rectangles did you use?

check.q: An L-shape is made of a 5 by 3 rectangle and a 2 by 4 rectangle. What is its area?
check.why: 5 × 3 = 15 and 2 × 4 = 8, so 15 + 8 = 23. Adding all the side lengths gives 14, which is not area.

check.q: A 6 by 6 square has a 2 by 3 rectangle cut from one corner. What area is left?
check.why: 36 − 6 = 30 square units. Adding the notch instead of subtracting gives 42.

check.q: Why do we split an L-shape into rectangles?
choices: Because we know a formula for rectangles
Because the shape becomes a square
check.why: Area = length × width works for each rectangle, and the pieces add up to the whole.

lessons.title: Find the Missing Side
lessons.mainIdea: If you know the area or perimeter and one side, work backward with division or subtraction to find the other side.
reading: Sometimes the answer is known and a side is missing. The class has 45 square feet of bed and one side is 5 feet. How long is the other side? Area = length × width, so 45 = length × 5. Ask: 5 times what makes 45? That is 45 ÷ 5 = 9. The missing side is 9 feet.

Perimeter works backward, too. A bed has a perimeter of 30 feet and a length of 10 feet. Half the perimeter is length plus width: 30 ÷ 2 = 15. Then 15 − 10 = 5. The width is 5 feet. Check: 2 × (10 + 5) = 30. It works.

Squares are special because both sides match. A square with an area of 64 square inches has a side that, times itself, gives 64. Since 8 × 8 = 64, the side is 8 inches. A common mistake is dividing 64 by 2 or by 4. Dividing by 4 gives a side only when you start from the perimeter, not the area.

words.d: a side length you must figure out from other facts about the shape
to start from the answer and undo each step to find what you started with

look.title: Undo the Multiplication
look.text: A rectangular rug has an area of 72 square feet and a width of 8 feet. Think: 8 times what equals 72? Since 8 × 9 = 72, the length is 9 feet. Now a different rug has a perimeter of 40 feet and a length of 12 feet. Half of 40 is 20. Then 20 − 12 = 8, so the width is 8 feet.
look.prompt: A third rug has an area of 60 square feet and a width of 6 feet. How long is it? Then find its perimeter.

check.q: A rectangle has an area of 56 square units and a width of 7. What is its length?
A rectangle has a perimeter of 24 units and a length of 9. What is its width?
check.why: Half of 24 is 12, so length + width = 12. Then 12 − 9 = 3.

check.q: A square has an area of 64 square cm. How long is one side?
check.why: 8 × 8 = 64, so each side is 8 cm. Dividing 64 by 4 gives 16, but that only works for perimeter.

lessons.title: Volume Is Counting Cubes
lessons.mainIdea: Volume is the number of unit cubes that pack a solid shape, counted layer by layer.
reading: The raised beds arrive as open boxes. How much soil fills one? Flat tiles cannot answer that, because soil fills space in three directions: length, width and height. Use *unit cubes* instead. A unit cube is 1 unit long, 1 unit wide and 1 unit tall. The number of cubes that pack a box is its *volume*.

Picture a box with a floor that is 4 cubes by 3 cubes. One *layer* of cubes covers the floor: 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. The box is 2 cubes tall, so it holds 2 layers. Count: 12 + 12 = 24 cubes. The volume is 24 *cubic units*. If each cube is 1 centimeter, the volume is 24 cubic centimeters.

The word cubic tells you it is volume, just as square tells you it is area. A common mistake is counting only the cubes you can see on the outside. Cubes hidden inside still count. Another mistake is counting the top layer twice. Count one full layer, then multiply by the number of layers.

words.d: a cube with every edge 1 unit long, like a centimeter cube
the number of unit cubes that fill a solid shape with no gaps
one flat level of cubes; a box that is 3 cubes tall has 3 layers
the label for volume; 24 cubic units means 24 unit cubes fit inside

look.title: Layers in a Box
look.text: A clear box has a floor that fits 5 cubes by 2 cubes. That is 10 cubes in the bottom layer. The box is 3 cubes tall. Stack: 10 in the first layer, 20 after the second, 30 after the third. The volume is 30 cubic units. Now picture a box whose floor fits 6 by 4 cubes and is 2 cubes tall.
look.prompt: How many cubes are in one layer of the second box? How many cubes fill it?

check.q: A box floor fits 5 cubes by 2 cubes, and the box is 3 cubes tall. What is its volume?
check.why: One layer is 5 × 2 = 10 cubes, and 3 layers make 10 × 3 = 30.

check.q: Which label belongs on a volume measured with centimeter cubes?
check.why: Volume counts cubes, so its label is cubic centimeters.

check.q: A box holds 18 unit cubes. Its bottom layer has 6 cubes. How many layers does it have?
check.why: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 layers, because 6 × 3 = 18.

lessons.title: The Volume Formula
lessons.mainIdea: For a box, volume = length × width × height, which is the same as the area of the floor times the height.
reading: Counting layers led to a shortcut. The floor of a box is a rectangle, so its area is length × width. Each layer holds that many cubes. Multiply by the height to count all the layers. The formula for a *rectangular prism*, the math name for a box, is Volume = length × width × height.

The class planter is 8 feet long, 2 feet wide and 1 foot deep. Volume = 8 × 2 × 1 = 16 cubic feet of soil. A bigger planter that is 6 by 4 by 5 has volume 6 × 4 × 5. Multiply in any order: 6 × 4 = 24, then 24 × 5 = 120 cubic feet. You can also do 4 × 5 = 20, then 20 × 6 = 120.

Think of it as *base area* times height. A base of 24 square feet with a height of 5 feet is 120 cubic feet. A common mistake is adding the three numbers, 6 + 4 + 5 = 15, or multiplying only two of them. Volume needs all three directions. When you are done, check that the label says cubic.

words.d: a box shape whose six faces are all rectangles
how tall a solid is, from its base straight up to its top
the area of the floor of a box; base area times height gives volume

rows: 8 ft by 2 ft by 1 ft planter
4 ft by 4 ft by 2 ft planter
6 ft by 3 ft by 2 ft planter
10 ft by 2 ft by 3 ft planter
look.cite: Volumes computed from length × width × height for each box
look.prompt: Bagged soil holds 2 cubic feet per bag. How many bags fill the 6 by 3 by 2 planter? How many fill all four?

check.q: A box is 3 units by 4 units by 5 units. What is its volume?
check.why: 3 × 4 = 12 and 12 × 5 = 60 cubic units. Adding 3 + 4 + 5 gives 12, which is wrong.

check.q: A cube has edges of 10 cm. What is its volume?
check.why: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 cubic centimeters. 100 is only the base area.

check.q: A planter is 8 feet by 2 feet by 1 foot. How much soil fills it?
check.why: 8 × 2 × 1 = 16 cubic feet. Adding the sides gives 11.

review.q: A rectangle is 7 feet by 4 feet. What is its area?
A rectangle is 7 feet by 4 feet. What is its perimeter?
Which is measured in cubic units?
review.why: Soil fills space in three directions, so it is a volume, measured in cubic units.

review.q: A square has a perimeter of 20 cm. What is its area?
review.why: Each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm, so the area is 5 × 5 = 25 square cm.

review.q: An L-shape is made of a 6 by 2 rectangle and a 3 by 3 square. What is its area?
A box is 5 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm. What is its volume?
A rectangle has an area of 36 square units and a width of 4. What is its perimeter?
Which two rectangles have the same perimeter but different areas?
review.why: 2 by 6 and 3 by 5 both have perimeter 16, but areas 12 and 15. The 4 by 4 and 2 by 8 have perimeters 16 and 20.
